messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Database Administrator
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Arguments: Arguments, Uncertainty: Uncertainty
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Physical Stress: Situations that put my body under stress, Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mei Lin was twenty-two years old and newly married when she nearly died on an interstate on-ramp. She had been driving them home from a weekend trip, her husband dozing in the passenger seat, when a pickup truck swerved into their lane without warning. She remembered the sound first—a long, tearing shriek of metal—and then the sensation of the car spinning, the world tipping sideways, the seatbelt cutting into her collarbone as her body tried to go somewhere else. The car came to rest against a guardrail, crumpled and smoking, and for what felt like an eternity she sat there, unable to move, certain that the next sound would be an explosion. Her husband was saying her name, over and over, but she could not answer. She could not make her mouth work. It was only later, in the emergency room, that she learned neither of them had been seriously injured. But by then, something in Mei Lin had already broken.

In the weeks that followed, she began to notice that certain things made her stomach drop. The name of the driver who had hit them—a name she had overheard the police officer say—began to surface everywhere. A colleague mentioned a cousin with that name. A character in a show her husband was watching had it. Each time, her chest would tighten, her palms would sweat, and she would have to leave the room. She started to avoid arguments with anyone, even trivial disagreements with her husband about groceries or weekend plans, because the raised voices sent her straight back into that spinning car, helpless and bracing for impact. Most of all, she came to dread uncertainty. A delayed text from her husband, an unconfirmed meeting time, a vague email from her boss—anything that left a question mark in her day felt like the floor about to fall away. She had come to believe, with a quiet and absolute certainty, that the crash had happened because of the way she acted. She should have checked her blind spot more carefully. She should have honked sooner. She should have been paying more attention. The thought circled her mind constantly, and she could not find a way out of it.

Mei Lin worked as a database administrator for a regional logistics company, a job she had once found satisfying because of its order and predictability. Now, that very order felt like a trap. Every time her system flagged an anomaly—a duplicate entry, a missing timestamp—her heart would race and she would freeze, unable to tell whether the problem was real or just her mind catastrophising. She began to avoid any physical activity that made her aware of her own body: no running, no cycling, no carrying heavy boxes of files at work. The sensation of a pounding heart or shortness of breath felt too much like the moments after the crash, when she had been certain she was dying. She stopped seeing her friends entirely, letting their calls go to voicemail and then deleting the messages unlistened. She told herself she was too busy, too tired, that they would not understand. What frightened her most was what she did in private. When the intrusive images became unbearable—the spinning, the shriek of metal, the moment of impact—she would dig her fingernails into her forearms or press the edge of a desk drawer into her thigh until the pain drowned out the memory. She had learned that physical pain was something she could control, something that ended when she chose to stop. The memories did not stop.

She had also come to see other people differently. Before the crash, she had trusted easily. Now she found herself scanning every interaction for signs of danger, for the moment someone might act carelessly and hurt her. Her husband had been in the car with her, had held her hand in the ambulance, but she found herself pulling away from him too. She would watch him drive and think, *He could kill us both.* She would hear him raise his voice on a phone call and feel her throat close. She was certain that people could not be trusted to keep her safe, because the one person who should have been watching the road had not, and now she was left with the wreckage. And beneath all of it, a deeper conviction that she would never forgive herself for not doing more to stop what happened. She had not screamed. She had not grabbed the wheel. She had simply sat there, frozen, as the truck bore down on them, and that failure felt like a permanent stain on who she was.

What finally brought Mei Lin to seek help was a moment at work. Her manager asked her to lead a small team on a new project, and the uncertainty of the request—the open-ended timeline, the unclear expectations—sent her into a panic that she could not hide. She excused herself to the bathroom and stood with her hands gripping the sink, breathing in short, shallow gasps, and she realised that she could not keep living this way. She made an appointment with a therapist the next day. She is terrified that talking about the crash will make it worse, that she will be swallowed whole by the memory. But she is also, beneath the fear, hoping for something she can barely name: a way to sit in a car without bracing for impact, a way to hear her husband's voice rise without feeling the world tip sideways, a way to forgive herself for being human.
